executive_summary: USD/JPY closed at 157.28 on 2026-09-29 and traded 158.19 on the valuation date; on the inverted convention a falling USD/JPY is a stronger yen, so the pair's 1M fall of 1.54%, 3M fall of 2.38% and 6M fall of 1.51% are yen GAINS, while the 1Y rise of 3.75% leaves the yen still weaker over twelve months. The dominant narrative is a collision between a hiking Bank of Japan - 1.25% since 2026-09-18, the highest since 1995, on a 7-2 vote - and a hiking Federal Reserve that took the target range to 3.75-4.00% on 2026-09-16 on a 12-0 vote, with UST 10y at 5.24% against a JGB 10y of 3.06%. The US-Japan 10y spread WIDENED about 39bp over the month (UST +51bp, JGB +12bp) and yet the yen outperformed every G10 currency over that month, a clean break in the pair's primary driver that only the late-July 2026 coordinated US-Japan intervention, the BoJ's second hike of the year and a 212.6K-contract CFTC positioning flip can explain. Valuation is the most extreme signal in the benchmarking set: the BIS REER at 66.02 for August 2026 is 28.8 points below the next-cheapest currency and has fallen a further 6.50 points over a year. The central tension is that the BoJ is tightening into a core CPI of 1.7%, below target for a seventh consecutive month and decelerating, because government energy subsidies are mechanically suppressing a headline print that sits beneath a producer price index running at 7.6%, with Brent 53.6% higher year-on-year and Japan importing 94.2% of its crude from the Middle East - a configuration in which the measured inflation case for hiking is weakest exactly when the currency case is strongest. We are Neutral tactically with conviction 2 and net weighted score -0.028, because the 275bp policy differential and a freshly crowded +72.0K net speculative long offset an under-priced 2026-10-30 Outlook Report; and Bullish strategically with conviction 3, because the differential's trajectory, the hedged-yield crossover behind life-insurer repatriation and a coordinated official put on the left tail all compound over one to six months in a way none of them does over four weeks. The strategic direction is shared with consensus, whose aggregated forecast is 151.62 at six months against our 151.00; the disagreement is about path, because we expect the near-term positioning liability to delay the move consensus expects to begin at once.

valuation.trade_weighted_assessment: The REER has fallen in nine of the last ten years and is now 34% below its own twenty-year average on BIS data, while every other currency in the set sits within roughly 15 points of 100. This is not a cyclical cheapness; it is a repricing of Japan's equilibrium real exchange rate by a market that spent two decades treating the yen as a free funding source.
valuation.what_is_priced_in: The current REER prices a permanent 275bp funding disadvantage, a permanently negative goods balance under a 98-dollar Brent, and a BoJ that normalises only glacially. It prices essentially none of the hedged-yield crossover that has already reversed life-insurer allocation, and none of the possibility that the BoJ's terminal rate exceeds 1.75%.
valuation.actionability: Strategic rather than tactical. A REER of 66.02 has been cheap for years without mean-reverting, so it is not a timing signal; it is the reason the strategic risk-reward is skewed 1.33:1 in the yen's favour and the reason the downside case stops at 162 rather than extending.

tactical.analysis: The Bank of Japan raised the uncollateralised overnight call rate target to 1.25% on 2026-09-18 on a 7-2 vote, the highest Japanese policy rate since 1995 and the second hike of 2026 after the move to 1.00% on 2026-07-30. That still leaves JPY with the lowest policy rate in the G10+SGD set bar the SNB's 0.00%, 335bp below the RBA's 4.60%, 325bp below Norges Bank's 4.50% and 275bp below the Fed's 4.00% target upper bound - 262.5bp on the 3.875% effective rate. The sovereign curve tells a more favourable story: JGB 2y is 1.93%, 5y 2.365%, 10y 3.05-3.07% and 30y 4.15% as of 2026-09-30, with the 10y up 141bp over a year and 2s10s at roughly +112bp. Against UST 2y at 4.92% and 10y at 5.24% the bilateral discounts are 299bp and 218bp respectively. The decisive tactical fact is that the 10y spread WIDENED about 39bp over the past month, as the UST 10y rose 51bp against a 12bp rise in the JGB, and USD/JPY nevertheless FELL 1.54% - the pair's primary driver and its price decoupled. That decoupling is why we do not translate a wide differential into a bearish tactical stance: the differential is not currently the binding constraint, intervention risk and positioning are. Against that, the 2026-10-30 meeting carries an Outlook Report and the market prices only about 25-38% of a hike there, against a Summary of Opinions in which a majority favour further tightening and one member argued for accelerating the pace. The honest reading is a level that is heavily yen-negative, a trajectory that is yen-positive, and a correlation that is temporarily suspended - offsetting forces, which is what Neutral is for.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the arithmetic that matters is not the level of the differential but its first derivative, and that derivative points one way. The Fed's own September projections put the end-2026 median at 4.1%, implying roughly one further 25bp move from a 3.75-4.00% range and then a plateau; the BoJ has moved 50bp in 2026 from a starting point of 0.75% and has three Outlook Report meetings inside the strategic window - 2026-10-30, 2027-01-22 and 2027-04-28 - at which to revise its forecast path upward. Two further BoJ hikes against a Fed on hold compresses the policy differential from 275bp to 225bp, and a market that comes to price a terminal BoJ rate of 2% rather than 1.5% would compress the 2y spread by considerably more than the spot moves it has delivered so far. The long end is already doing this: the JGB 10y has risen 141bp over a year to 3.06%, has crossed above the German Bund yield, and now trades 259bp ABOVE the Swiss Confederation 10y - Japan has stopped being the world's lowest-yielding major sovereign, which is a structural change in the funding-currency proposition rather than a cyclical one. Carry economics confirm it: short JPY against AUD earns 335bp a year, about 10.1 AUD/JPY pips a month, against an AUD/JPY ATR14 of 85 pips, so a single average day erases eight days of carry, and AUD/JPY's 4.01% one-month fall destroyed roughly fourteen months of it. The one pair where JPY now earns carry is CHF/JPY at +125bp, the clean expression of BoJ-versus-SNB divergence. The strategic risk is a Takaichi administration that leans on the Bank, but the September hike was delivered under that administration, which is the best available evidence on independence.

tactical.analysis: Japan's August 2026 national CPI, released 2026-09-17, printed 1.9% headline, 1.7% on the BoJ's preferred core measure excluding fresh food, and 1.9% on core-core excluding fresh food and energy. Core eased from 1.8% and has now sat BELOW the 2% target for a seventh consecutive month - the Bank is hiking into a disinflating core, which on the face of it is a yen-negative data flow because it undercuts the case for the next move. The face of it is misleading. Electricity prices fell 2.4% year-on-year against -0.1% the prior month because of government energy subsidies, mechanically suppressing the headline while Brent sits 53.6% higher year-on-year and Japan imports 94.2% of its crude from the Middle East; the producer price index is running at 7.6% year-on-year against a consumer core of 1.7%, a 5.7-point pipeline that has not passed through, and the corporate services price index at 3.7% beat forecast and is accelerating. Growth is bifurcated in a way that resists a single stance: Q2 GDP rose 0.4% quarter-on-quarter and 1.4% annualised, beating forecast, but external demand contributed 0.5pp while private consumption contributed exactly zero and capital expenditure fell 0.9%. The October Tankan showed large manufacturers at +24, the highest since March 2018 and a sixth straight rise, but it MISSED the +25 consensus and large non-manufacturers fell to +35 from 37. August industrial production fell 1.7% month-on-month against a +1.4% forecast, retail sales rose 2.7% against 3.3% expected, household spending fell 3.6% year-on-year, and the Leading Index missed at 117.7. The tactical data flow is therefore genuinely two-sided - a hot pipeline and a cold consumer - and neither side is winning.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market has priced the core deceleration as a reason to fade the BoJ, which is why only a quarter to a third of an October hike is in the curve. It has not priced the subsidy mechanics: the suppressed electricity component reverses into the print when subsidies roll off, and a 7.6% PPI sitting above a 1.7% core is an unpassed cost shock, not an absent one. Our expectation for the next core print is 1.7-1.9%, in line, with the asymmetry to the upside from 2027.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the question is whether Japan's inflation regime has durably shifted, and the evidence is genuinely split between the price-setting and the demand sides. On price-setting the case is strong: the October Tankan reports firms expecting 2.6% inflation three years ahead, which is above target and anchored upward, with capital spending plans at +11.3%; the 2026 Shunto settled at 5.01%, the fourth consecutive year above 5%; and the producer price index at 7.6% against a 1.7% consumer core leaves a 5.7-point margin of unpassed cost that an energy subsidy programme is currently absorbing on the government's balance sheet rather than the consumer's. On the demand side the case is weak and getting weaker: GDP year-on-year of 0.73% is the lowest in the G10+SGD set, private consumption contributed zero in Q2, household spending fell 3.6% year-on-year, real wages have been negative for a fourth consecutive year despite nominal settlements above 5%, and Japan's demographics impose a structural ceiling on potential growth near 0.5-1%. The export engine is real but narrow - electronic components including semiconductors rose 52.3% to 894.1bn yen on AI chip demand - and both South Korea and Taiwan out-exported Japan in H1 2026 for the first time, which says the competitive position is deteriorating even as the cycle flatters it. For the currency the net is close to zero: enough inflation persistence to keep the BoJ moving, not enough growth to make Japan an attractive destination for capital on fundamentals alone.

tactical.analysis: The global risk tape is benign in level and deteriorating at the margin, which for a safe-haven currency is a genuinely ambiguous configuration. VIX closed at 16.07 on 2026-09-28, a low absolute level sitting around the 35th-40th percentile of the post-2010 distribution, but it rose 1.64 points over the month. US investment grade spreads at 83bp are historically tight and barely moved; US high yield at 302bp widened 42bp over the same month. IG holding while HY widens and VIX ticks up is the textbook early signature of risk appetite cracking at the low-quality end rather than a broad risk-off, and it is not yet enough to drive safe-haven demand. The yen's textbook behaviour - the strongest negative VIX correlation in G10, amplified by carry unwinds because carry traders are structurally short JPY - is intact in mechanism but has not been the operative channel: over the past month the yen beat every G10 currency, with AUD/JPY down 4.01%, NZD/JPY down 6.11% and CHF/JPY down 4.54%, in a tape where equities held and VIX stayed at 16. A safe haven outperforming in risk-on is a regime break from the currency brief's historical characterisation, and it says the yen's September move was policy and positioning, not fear. For the tactical horizon that cuts both ways: the yen has already captured its move without needing risk aversion, so a benign tape removes a tailwind it was not using, while a genuine risk event would deliver an outsized move because the channel is unspent. Gold at 4,182 dollars, down 6.0% over a month from an extraordinary 2026 peak, points the same way - the crisis premium built during the Iran conflict is draining, not rebuilding.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the risk factor is an asymmetry argument rather than a directional one, and the asymmetry favours the yen. VIX at 16.07 and IG at 83bp leave far more room to widen than to tighten: IG spreads of 83bp are near the floor of their post-crisis range, and the distribution of six-month changes from such a starting point is heavily skewed to widening. The yen is the highest-beta G10 beneficiary of any such move, both through the classic repatriation channel - Japanese investors hold roughly 3.5 trillion dollars of foreign securities and sell them to buy yen in stress - and through the carry-unwind channel, in which traders who are short yen to fund higher-yielding positions must buy it back. The second channel is materially less loaded than it was: CFTC speculative positioning has flipped from -92.2K net short to +72.0K net long in three weeks and open interest fell 30% in a single week, so the violence of a squeeze is lower than at any point this cycle. That reduces the magnitude but not the direction. The specific tail that matters is the Iran file: the ceasefire of 2026-04-08 holds, Hormuz traffic has recovered to 13.2 million barrels a day and Saudi Arabia has restored half its East-West pipeline capacity, but US-Iran negotiations over control of the waterway remain unresolved and shipping remains far below pre-war levels. A re-escalation is a double-edged event for Japan - safe-haven bid against a terms-of-trade shock - but historically the FX channel dominates the trade channel on a one-to-three-month view. High yield widening 42bp in a month while equities held is the first observable crack, and it is the one we would track.

Over four weeks a VIX of 16 simply fails to generate a safe-haven bid, and the yen has already made its move without one. Over six months the starting point is what matters: credit at 83bp and VIX at 16 cannot tighten much further and can widen a great deal, and the yen is the instrument with the highest beta to that widening. The transition is not dated - it requires a shock - which is why strategic confidence is only 55.

tactical.analysis: Speculative positioning in the yen has just completed the most violent reversal of this cycle and now sits on the wrong side for the first time in years. CFTC non-commercial net positions went from -63.3K contracts in the release of 2026-08-28 to -92.2K on 2026-09-04, then to +10.8K on 2026-09-11, +120.4K on 2026-09-18 and back to +72.0K on 2026-09-25 - a 212.6K-contract swing from short to long in two weeks, followed by a 48.4K give-back. The currency brief sets the historical extreme for yen net longs at +80K contracts; +120.4K breached it outright and +72.0K sits just inside. The disaggregated cached tranche for 2026-09-22 shows where the long actually sits: leveraged funds are net +7,423, essentially flat, while asset managers are net +41,629 and dealers are net -108,284. That composition matters more than the headline. The fast money that drove the squeeze has already taken its profit and gone home; what remains is a real-money long which is stickier, less leveraged and far less likely to be forced out, but which also provides no further buying power. Open interest collapsed from 542,802 contracts on 2026-09-15 to 378,701 on 2026-09-22, a 30% fall in a single week, which is the signature of positions being closed rather than flipped. The tactical implication is unambiguous and it is bearish for the yen: the short base that fuelled a 1.54% one-month rally has been consumed, the market is now modestly long into an event calendar it prices at only a quarter to a third hawkish, and the pain trade for the first time in this cycle is a weaker yen rather than a stronger one.

strategic.analysis: Positioning is a mean-reverting tactical variable, and over one to six months the flow that matters in the yen is institutional rather than speculative. The structural development of 2025-26 is that long-dated JGBs now out-yield currency-hedged US Treasuries once the 3-4% annual hedge cost is applied, which has reversed the two-decade outflow from Japanese life insurers and pension funds. Lifer hedge ratios run at 50-60% of foreign assets, so the decision to stop adding unhedged foreign bonds and to rotate into domestic paper removes a persistent structural yen seller and replaces it with a buyer; foreign official holdings of US Treasuries fell to a thirty-year low of 13% by July 2026 as the same arithmetic played out across official portfolios. The carry trade that sits on the other side is large but bounded - estimates range from 261bn dollars of direct cross-border yen borrowing to roughly 1 trillion dollars including derivatives - and its economics have deteriorated: every JPY cross except CHF/JPY fell over the past month while paying 100-335bp a year to be held. By the end of the strategic window the Japanese fiscal year-end of 2027-03-31 adds its documented repatriation impulse on top. The speculative long that is a tactical liability becomes a strategic irrelevance once it normalises, which it typically does within four to eight weeks, leaving the institutional flow as the signal. Weekly securities data show the transition is not yet linear - Japanese buying of foreign bonds resumed at +1,082.9bn yen in the week to 2026-09-16 - so this is a trend with noise, not a switch.

factors.horizon_split_explanation: The stances invert because the two horizons read different flows. Speculative positioning at +72.0K contracts is a four-week liability and nothing more; institutional repatriation driven by hedge-cost arithmetic is a six-month asset and barely registers inside four weeks. The crossover is the point at which the speculative long normalises toward zero, historically four to eight weeks after an extreme, which places it in late October or November - conveniently close to the 2026-10-30 Outlook Report.
factors.contrarian_analysis_tactical: Positioning is stretched, but on the long side for the first time this cycle - the mirror image of the setup that has characterised the yen for a decade. The currency brief's threshold for an extreme net long is +80K contracts; the 2026-09-18 print of +120.4K cleared it and the current +72.0K sits just beneath. The trigger for an unwind is simple and dated: a BoJ hold on 2026-10-30 without a hawkish Outlook Report revision, or a strong US payrolls print that re-widens the front-end spread. Severity would be moderate rather than violent, because leveraged funds at +7,423 are effectively flat and the long is held by asset managers at +41,629 who do not run stops - a liquidation of a real-money long drips out over weeks rather than gapping in hours, which is the opposite of the July 2024 analogue where a leveraged short unwound 15 big figures in weeks. The contrarian case against our own bearish tactical stance is that open interest has already fallen 30% in a week, so much of the excess has been purged, and that the dealers' -108,284 position means the street is short yen and would have to buy it back on any hawkish surprise.
factors.contrarian_analysis_strategic: Strategically the contrarian signal reverses sign. A market that has just flipped from -92.2K to +72.0K has, in the process, destroyed the structural yen short that suppressed the currency for years - and a destroyed short does not rebuild quickly when every JPY cross except CHF/JPY has fallen while paying 100-335bp a year to hold. The historical analogue is 2024, when a similar flip preceded a sustained period in which the yen no longer traded as a pure funding currency. The contrarian risk to our strategic bullish stance is that the carry trade rebuilds faster than we expect if the BoJ stalls at 1.25% and the Fed delivers one more hike: with VIX at 16.07 and realised vol on the crosses in the 7.8-9.1% range, the conditions for carry accumulation are present even though the returns currently are not. The honest statement of the other side is that 261bn to 1 trillion dollars of carry positioning has reconstituted itself many times before on exactly this configuration, and the only thing stopping it this cycle is that JGBs finally pay something.

tactical.analysis: Japan's external accounts split into a headline that flatters the yen and a marginal flow that does not. The current account surplus is 5.03% of GDP on the 2026-Q2 vintage and the first half of 2026 produced a 17.43 trillion yen surplus against 14.23 trillion a year earlier, so the aggregate position is both large and improving. But the composition is the point: July's 2,988.9bn yen surplus rested on a primary income balance of 4,289.6bn yen, which is investment income on Japan's net international investment position of roughly 3.3 trillion dollars and is overwhelmingly reinvested abroad rather than converted into yen. The goods balance, which IS converted, is in deficit - 1,105.6bn yen in August 2026, the fourth consecutive monthly deficit and the largest since January 2026, against a 1,052.6bn forecast. The driver is energy: crude oil imports rose 58.7% to 1.191 trillion yen and total mineral fuel imports rose 38.4% to 2.464 trillion yen, with Brent at 98.48 dollars on the valuation date, 53.6% higher than a year ago, and Japan sourcing 94.2% of its crude from the Middle East. Exports are strong - 10.05 trillion yen, up 19.3% year-on-year and a twelfth consecutive rise, led by electronic components up 52.3% on AI chip demand - but imports grew faster at 28.0%. Over the tactical window the operative mechanism is the monthly trade settlement flow, which is a persistent yen seller, and the 2026-10-07 current account release is the next test.

The surplus is income reinvested offshore; the deficit is goods settled in spot. We expect the 2026-10-07 current account print to stay in surplus and the next trade print to stay in deficit, which is a configuration the market reads as neutral and we read as mildly yen-negative.

strategic.analysis: The strategic external case against the yen rests on a terms-of-trade shock that is structural in origin and has not reversed. The 2026 Iran war closed the Strait of Hormuz, disrupting 20% of global oil supply and, after the 2026-03-18 strike on Qatar's Ras Laffan facility which cut Qatari capacity by 17%, driving Asian LNG spot prices up more than 140%. Brent peaked at 118.35 dollars on 2026-03-31, fell to 71.57 by 2026-07-01 and has recovered to 98.48 - 53.6% above a year ago - with Hormuz traffic still below pre-war levels and US-Iran negotiations over the waterway unresolved. For an economy that imports 99% of its oil and most of its gas, and 94.2% of its crude from the region in question, this is a permanent transfer of real income abroad that shows up as a goods deficit every month. Four consecutive monthly deficits with crude imports up 58.7% is the mechanism operating. The offsets are real and are why confidence is 58 rather than higher: the primary income surplus grew to 4,289.6bn yen in July and provides a floor the trade deficit cannot breach, the AI semiconductor export cycle lifted electronic components 52.3%, and the current account surplus widened year-on-year DESPITE the energy shock. But the competitive trend is adverse - both South Korea and Taiwan out-exported Japan in H1 2026 for the first time - and the strategic weight on this factor is 0.16, the second-highest in the framework, precisely because cumulative balance-of-payments flows compound.

Over four weeks a single trade print moves little; over six months four-plus consecutive deficits at 58.7% crude import growth compound into a measurable transfer. The confidence gap of two points reflects that the strategic case rests on an energy level that has already happened rather than on a forecast of further increases.

tactical.analysis: The gap between what the Bank of Japan says and what the market pays for is the factor, and it is currently the widest it has been this cycle. The 2026-09-18 statement guided that the Bank will continue raising policy interest rates and gradually adjust monetary accommodation as underlying inflation approaches 2%, and framed the move as preemptive action against upside risks to avoid rapid hikes later. The Summary of Opinions released 2026-09-30 is more explicit still: a majority favoured further hikes, one member argued for accelerating the pace if inflation deviates upward, another wanted to move closer to the target relatively soon, and a third named Middle East crude as an inflation risk. Against that, OIS carries roughly 25-38% for a 25bp move on 2026-10-30 and consensus is a hold. The market is discounting the BoJ's own stated reaction function by something like 15-25bp over the next two meetings. Two things moderate the stance. First, the 7-2 vote - with Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato dissenting - raises the bar for a back-to-back move, and the market responded to the Summary of Opinions by scaling back October hike bets and taking USD/JPY to 157.87. Second, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi leads an expansionary-fiscal administration widely assumed to prefer accommodation, with the Cabinet Office urging the Bank to weigh the cumulative effect of past hikes and Economy Minister Minoru Kiuchi reportedly concerned about government funding costs. The decisive counter-evidence is that the September hike was delivered anyway, under that administration, by a Bank whose history is of under-delivering on telegraphed moves and over-delivering on surprises.

We think the true probability is closer to 40-45% given an Outlook Report that provides the vehicle for a forecast upgrade and a Summary of Opinions whose median member is hawkish. strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the BoJ has three Outlook Report meetings - 2026-10-30, 2027-01-22 and 2027-04-28 - and each is a scheduled opportunity to revise the forecast CPI path upward and, with it, the market's estimate of the terminal rate. That institutional cadence is the mechanism by which guidance becomes price. Credibility is improving from a low base: the Bank's communication is still the most opaque in G10 and its two most consequential policy shifts, the December 2022 yield curve control adjustment and the 2024 abolition, both surprised markets, but Governor Ueda has now delivered two hikes in 2026 against persistent political pressure and published a Summary of Opinions that reads more hawkishly than the vote. The distribution around the Outlook Reports is therefore fat-tailed toward hawkish outcomes, which is the opposite of the symmetric risk the curve assumes. The structural offset is the Takaichi administration: an expansionary fiscal programme including a food tax cut, a 2026-10-05 parliamentary address pledging to respond swiftly to unexpected developments in markets, and a standing market assumption that she will press the Bank to stay accommodative - an assumption that has contributed directly to yen weakness. A separate and underappreciated element of guidance is the Ministry of Finance: Katayama's statement that Japan will not hesitate to conduct further coordinated interventions, alongside US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's confirmation that the July action countered disorderly yen movements, converts intervention from a unilateral Japanese threat into a two-government commitment. That is a form of forward guidance on the exchange rate itself, and it is new.

tactical.analysis: The defining event-risk fact for the yen is that it now carries an explicit, demonstrated, two-government floor. On late July 2026 Japan and the United States conducted their first coordinated FX intervention since 2011, with Japan selling roughly 8.45 trillion yen of foreign currency - 52.8 to 59 billion dollars, with Bank of Japan data suggesting about 58.97 billion - and the US Treasury contributing an estimated maximum of 26.3 billion dollars, driving USD/JPY from approximately 164 to a near-three-month high of 155.20. SOURCE DISCREPANCY, FLAGGED: one account dates the operation 2026-07-31, another describes a New York-session intervention on the Thursday with joint confirmation published 2026-08-02/03; the size, the levels and the joint character agree across both accounts, the calendar date does not, and the confidence on this factor has been lowered accordingly. Options-desk accounts describe two rounds within twenty-four hours in late July, taking the pair from 163.00 to 157.80 and then from 160.51 to 158.90. Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama has said Japan will not hesitate to conduct further coordinated interventions and remains in close communication with the US Treasury; Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed the action countered disorderly yen movements. The practical effect over a two-to-four week window is a truncated left tail for the yen: a move back toward 162-164 invites a second operation, which caps the realistic bearish-JPY outcome far more tightly than the bullish one. The dated calendar inside the window is dense - 2026-10-02 US payrolls, 2026-10-05 the Takaichi parliamentary address, 2026-10-07 the Japanese current account, 2026-10-28 the FOMC - with the 2026-10-30 BoJ Outlook Report immediately beyond it. The live tail is Iran: the 2026-04-08 ceasefire holds and Hormuz flows have recovered to 13.2 million barrels a day, but US-Iran negotiations over control of the waterway remain unresolved and a re-escalation is a two-sided event for Japan, safe-haven bid against energy shock, in which the FX channel has historically dominated over a one-to-three month view.

tactical.what_is_priced: The options market prices the October event cluster through a 59bp inversion between 1-month and 6-month implied vol, which is thin for a calendar containing both an FOMC and a BoJ Outlook Report. Intervention risk appears substantially under-priced in the tails: the market treats 160 as a soft ceiling without paying much for the possibility that a second coordinated operation is larger and better telegraphed than the first.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the intervention put is the single most important structural change to the yen's risk distribution in a decade, because a unilateral MoF operation is a threat the market routinely tests while a joint US-Japan operation is a policy commitment it does not. That asymmetry truncates the bearish-yen tail at roughly 162-164 without truncating the bullish one, which is worth a modest positive stance on its own. The offsetting risks are fiscal and political rather than external. PM Takaichi's expansionary programme runs into the FY2027 budget season in December, Fitch has said publicly it will scrutinise that budget for the balance between growth and fiscal discipline, and JGB yields have risen in consecutive double-digit quarterly increments as the market disciplines spending signals. US-Japan trade friction over autos and semiconductors is a standing irritant, and the 550 billion dollar Japan-US investment package is a known driver of cross-currency basis that could pressure yen funding. The geopolitical tails that would move the yen most are China-Taiwan and a Hormuz re-escalation; both are yen-positive through the safe-haven channel and the first is unambiguously so, while the second is contaminated by Japan's 94.2% Middle East crude dependence. Assigning probabilities: we put a second coordinated intervention at roughly 20% over six months conditional on USD/JPY revisiting 162, a Hormuz re-escalation at roughly 15%, and a Japanese snap election at roughly 15%. None individually dominates; together they skew the distribution toward yen strength.

strategic.analysis: The strategic fiscal case against the yen is the fiscal-monetary circularity closing at precisely the moment the administration wants to spend. Japan's debt dynamics have been sustainable for thirty years on three conditions: domestic ownership near 90%, a Bank of Japan absorbing roughly half the stock, and yields pinned near zero by deflation. Two of those three are now changing simultaneously. The 10-year yield has risen 141bp in a year to 3.06% and the 30-year sits at 4.15%; with a debt stock near 260% of GDP, each 100bp on the average yield eventually costs roughly 2% of GDP in debt service, which on current trajectories consumes the fiscal space the Takaichi programme requires. The programme itself - including a food tax cut - runs into the FY2027 budget in December, and Fitch has publicly stated it will review that budget for the balance between growth and fiscal discipline. Yields are already on track for consecutive double-digit quarterly increases, and the market has twice this quarter demonstrated it will move the long end on fiscal signals in both directions. The currency transmission is the part that is often missed: higher JGB yields are yen-positive through the differential channel but yen-negative through the sovereign-risk channel, and which dominates depends on whether the rise is driven by policy normalisation or by term premium. A 30y at 4.15% against a 2y at 1.93% - a 222bp spread - says the market is increasingly pricing term premium rather than policy. Confidence is only 56 because ratings are stable, auctions are clearing, and domestic ownership remains the shock absorber it has always been.

It has had nine months to absorb a Fed that adds reserves while hiking - a combination that supports risk assets and therefore carry, which is yen-negative, while removing the funding-squeeze channel that has periodically forced violent yen rallies. strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the funding channel is potentially the largest flow mechanism in this dossier, though not the most certain, and it runs through hedge costs rather than through stress. Japanese life insurers and pension funds hedge 50-60% of their foreign asset holdings, and at hedge costs of 3-4% a year the pickup on currency-hedged US Treasuries over domestic JGBs has gone negative now that the 10-year JGB yields 3.06% and the 30-year 4.15%. The observable consequence is already in the data: the repatriation turn became visible from mid-2025, and foreign official holdings of US Treasuries fell to a thirty-year low of 13% by July 2026 as the same arithmetic propagated. Fed balance-sheet policy is not part of this case: quantitative tightening ended on 2025-12-01 and the reserve-management bill purchases restated on 2026-09-16 are a continuation that was already in place when the prior dossier rated this factor Bearish. Hedge costs are set by the short-rate differential, and that is not yet falling - the Fed hiked to 3.75-4.00% on 2026-09-16 and the September SEP median of 4.1% implies one more move - so the case rests on the crossover holding at today's hedge costs and on every BoJ hike improving the domestic alternative. That is a structurally yen-positive flow that does not require a risk event, a carry unwind or an intervention to operate - it only requires the arithmetic to stay where it is. The offsets are real: the dollar sits on the exceptionalism side of the smile with the broad index up 1.88 on the month, December year-end dollar demand reliably widens the basis seasonally, and Japan's 550 billion dollar US investment package is a known source of structural dollar demand that pushes the basis the other way. But none of those changes the direction of the hedged-yield comparison, which is the variable that moves 3.5 trillion dollars of Japanese foreign securities. Weekly data do not yet confirm it: Japanese investors bought 1,082.9bn yen of foreign bonds in the week to 2026-09-16, above the +1,000bn threshold this dossier treats as evidence the crossover is not yet binding. We rate this Bullish at only 52: the crossover is a current, quantified condition, but hedge costs can still rise before they fall, the flow evidence is mixed and the dollar sits on the exceptionalism side of the smile.

The Fed's September projections put the end-2026 median at 4.1%, implying roughly one further hike from 3.75-4.00% and then a plateau, while the BoJ has moved 50bp this year and holds three Outlook Report meetings inside the window on 2026-10-30, 2027-01-22 and 2027-04-28. Two BoJ hikes against a Fed on hold compresses the policy gap from 275bp to 225bp. More importantly, with the ten-year JGB at 3.06% and the thirty-year at 4.15%, long-dated Japanese government bonds now out-yield currency-hedged US Treasuries once 3-4% annual hedge costs are applied, which reverses the two-decade outflow from life insurers running 50-60% hedge ratios against roughly 3.5 trillion dollars of foreign securities. Fed balance-sheet policy is not a new input - quantitative tightening ended on 2025-12-01 and reserve-management bill purchases simply continue - so the funding case rests on the crossover holding at current hedge costs, with every BoJ hike improving the domestic alternative; it is held at low confidence because the Fed may hike once more before hedge costs plateau. These factors reinforce rather than conflict - Policy drives Guidance drives Funding - while the conflicting factor, External Balance, is a real and persistent drag: four consecutive monthly trade deficits with crude imports up 58.7% and Brent 53.6% higher year-on-year on an economy that sources 94.2% of its crude from the Middle East. What is priced is a forward curve at -296bp annualised implying 154.95 at six months, against an aggregated institutional consensus of 151.62 at six months and 145.40 by Q1 2027. What we expect is 151.00 at six months: a +395-pip edge to the forward, essentially in line with the six-month consensus, and roughly 560 pips less bullish than the Q1 2027 consensus. The disagreement with consensus is therefore about path and terminal level rather than direction, which is a narrower divergence than a casual reading of the forward curve suggests. The path of least resistance is a grind lower in USD/JPY punctuated by the three Outlook Reports and amplified by the 2027-03-31 fiscal year-end repatriation window. Conviction is 3 because three independent mechanisms - policy compression, hedged-yield crossover and a coordinated official put - point the same way while the valuation signal is the most extreme in the set, with the BIS REER at 66.02 some 28.8 points below the next-cheapest currency. It is not 4 because the 200-week moving average at 149.09 rises into the target and because a 260%-of-GDP debt stock meets an expansionary December budget inside the window.

g10_ranking.commentary: JPY ranks 3 of 11 on strategic net weighted score (+0.250), behind NOK (+0.274), SEK (+0.258) and ahead of SGD (+0.216), AUD (+0.031), NZD (-0.066), GBP (-0.091), USD (-0.182), CHF (-0.257), EUR (-0.270), CAD (-0.365). The ranking rests on the most extreme valuation in the set - a BIS REER of 66.02, some 28.8 points below the next-cheapest currency - a central bank with more remaining tightening than any peer, and a coordinated official floor. It loses to NOK, which pairs a 4.50% policy rate and a hiking central bank with a 19.6%-of-GDP current account surplus, and to SEK by only 0.008 points, well inside the uncertainty of this dossier's low-confidence USD Liquidity call. It beats USD because the Fed is at or near its terminal rate while the BoJ has three forecast rounds left, and beats CHF decisively because JPY is the only currency in the set that earns carry against the franc.

Volatility should run above the 8.72% six-month implied throughout, because the intervention put produces gaps rather than drift and three binary policy events sit in the path. consensus_divergence.consensus_view: Sell-side consensus is for the BoJ to hold at 1.25% on 2026-10-30, and the aggregated institutional forecast for USD/JPY is materially yen-BULLISH: 155.39 at one month, 153.75 at three months, 151.62 at six months and 145.40 by Q1 2027, derived from weighted bank research with outlier filtering. VERIFICATION NOTE: an earlier draft of this dossier cited a consensus near 158.34; the cited aggregator does not carry that figure and the levels above are what it actually publishes. The correction moves consensus from mildly yen-bearish to clearly yen-bullish and is the single largest change made at the verification stage.
consensus_divergence.our_view: We are MORE bearish on the yen than consensus at one and three months, and LESS bullish at six. Over four weeks we see USD/JPY near 158.00 in a 156.00-159.50 band against a consensus of 155.39. At three months we see 154.50 against 153.75. At six months we see 151.00 against 151.62 - essentially in line - and by Q1 2027 consensus reaches 145.40, which is 5.6 big figures beyond our base case.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Approximately 261 pips MORE yen-bearish than consensus at one month (158.00 versus 155.39), 75 pips more yen-bearish at three months, 62 pips more yen-bullish at six months, and roughly 560 pips LESS yen-bullish than the consensus Q1 2027 projection of 145.40. Against the forward curve the six-month edge is +395 pips.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: Our disagreement with consensus is about PATH and TERMINAL LEVEL, not direction. Consensus and we both expect a stronger yen over six months; consensus expects the move to start immediately and to run further. We think it starts later, because the market underweights the near-term positioning liability - a 212.6K-contract flip from -92.2K short to +120.4K long leaves no short base to squeeze and a +72.0K real-money long to digest - and we think it stops nearer 151 because the 200-week moving average rises into roughly 151 by end-March 2027 and has never been breached. Where we are more constructive than consensus is on the mechanism rather than the magnitude: the market underweights four things. First, the hedged-yield crossover: with the JGB 10y at 3.06% and the 30y at 4.15%, long-dated Japanese government bonds now out-yield currency-hedged US Treasuries after 3-4% annual hedge costs, which reverses a two-decade outflow from institutions holding roughly 3.5 trillion dollars of foreign securities at 50-60% hedge ratios. Second, the hedge-cost path: on its own September projections the Fed is one move from terminal, so hedge costs stop rising precisely when every BoJ hike improves the domestic alternative - a short-rate effect, not a balance-sheet one, since quantitative tightening has been over since 2025-12-01. Third, the energy subsidy mechanics: a core CPI of 1.7% sits beneath a producer price index of 7.6% because the government is absorbing an energy shock on its own balance sheet, and that suppression has an expiry date. Fourth, the character of the intervention put: a joint US-Japan operation co-signed by the US Treasury is a different instrument from a unilateral MoF threat, and the market still prices it as the latter.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: USD/JPY at 151.00 against a six-month forward outright of 154.95 is a 395-pip edge, and the tactical call of 158.00 against a consensus 155.39 is a 261-pip edge over four weeks. The cleanest strategic expression, short CHF/JPY, pairs the directional view with a positive 125bp carry rather than paying for the position.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: There are two ways to be wrong and they are not symmetric. If consensus is right on timing, the yen strengthens immediately and the tactical call loses roughly 261 pips over four weeks. If consensus is right on magnitude and USD/JPY reaches 145.40 by Q1 2027, the strategic call leaves roughly 560 pips on the table without losing money. The genuine loss case is a BoJ stall at 1.25% with two further Fed hikes, which takes USD/JPY to 162 and costs the strategic view roughly 472 pips, concentrated in the December-to-February stretch where the FY2027 budget and the political constraint on the Bank coincide.

factors_changed.reason: The BoJ delivered the expected hike to 1.25% on 2026-09-18, but the US-Japan 10-year spread WIDENED approximately 39bp over the month as the UST 10y rose 51bp. The level of the differential now offsets its trajectory over four weeks. Strategically the stance stays Bullish and confidence rises from 60 to 66 because the hike was delivered and three Outlook Reports remain.

factors_changed.new_stance: Neutral at both horizons (58 tactical, 60 strategic)
factors_changed.reason: Core CPI ex fresh food eased to 1.7% and is now below the 2% target for a seventh consecutive month, while private consumption contributed zero to Q2 GDP and the October Tankan missed consensus at +24. The inflation case for further tightening weakened even as the pipeline (PPI 7.6%) firmed.

US high yield spreads widened 42bp over the month to 302bp while IG held at 83bp and VIX rose to 16.07 - the first observable crack in risk appetite. The strategic asymmetry from a tight starting point now favours the yen.

The single largest change in the dossier. CFTC net speculative positioning flipped 212.6K contracts from -92.2K short to +120.4K long in two weeks before settling at +72.0K, and open interest fell 30% in the week to 2026-09-22. The structural short that supported the bullish tactical case has been consumed.

Stance unchanged, confidence reduced at both horizons. The H1 2026 current account surplus widened to 17.43 trillion yen from 14.23 trillion a year earlier despite the energy shock, and electronic component exports rose 52.3%, which partially offsets a fourth consecutive monthly trade deficit.

The coordinated US-Japan character of the late-July 2026 intervention has been confirmed by both Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, each of whom said their government would not hesitate to participate in further joint intervention, converting a unilateral threat into a two-government commitment that truncates the bearish-yen tail at both horizons.

Auctions are clearing - the late-September 40-year sale drew the strongest demand since 2020 - and JGB yields fell across the curve on 2026-09-30 on a fiscal-reassurance report, removing any tactical catalyst. Strategic confidence eased because ratings remain stable at Moody's A1, S&P A+ and Fitch A.

Not driven by any change in Fed balance-sheet policy: the FOMC announced on 2025-10-29 that runoff would end on 2025-12-01, and the 2026-09-16 implementation note continues the reserve-management bill purchases the prior dossier already recorded. Tactically the Bearish reading is withdrawn because the 2026-09-16 hike raised the price of dollars while funding stress stayed absent (derived 3-month basis about -21bp), leaving abundant-but-expensive dollars with no net signal. Strategically the stance moves to a low-confidence Bullish on a re-weighting of existing conditions rather than a new event: with the JGB 10y at 3.06% and the 30y at 4.15%, long JGBs out-yield currency-hedged Treasuries at 3-4% hedge costs, a crossover the prior dossier treated as a possible reversal channel rather than the base case. Confidence is held at 52 because hedge costs may still rise with one more Fed hike and weekly flow data do not yet confirm repatriation.

conviction_change.explanation: Tactical conviction is unchanged at 2 but the stance moved from Bullish to Neutral, with the net weighted score falling from +0.127 to -0.028 as the positioning tailwind became a headwind. Strategic conviction rose from 2 to 3 and the net score from +0.094 to +0.250, driven mainly by two factor flips: USD Liquidity from Bearish 55 to a low-confidence Bullish 52 on the hedged-yield crossover (about +0.128), and Risk Appetite from Neutral to Bullish on the asymmetry from tight credit spreads. The USD Liquidity change does not reflect any change in Fed balance-sheet policy, which has been unchanged since quantitative tightening ended on 2025-12-01; without it the strategic score would sit near +0.12 and conviction would be 2, so strategic conviction 3 is only as secure as that low-confidence call.

new_catalysts: The 2026-10-30 BoJ meeting carries an Outlook Report, making it a scheduled forecast-revision vehicle rather than an ordinary decision
The FY2027 budget compilation in December 2026, with Fitch publicly committed to reviewing it for fiscal discipline
PM Takaichi's 2026-10-05 parliamentary policy address setting out the expansionary fiscal programme
The remaining Fed hike implied by the September SEP median of 4.1%, which sets the peak in Japanese hedge costs and therefore the timing of institutional repatriation
The 2027-03-31 Japanese fiscal year-end now falls inside the strategic window, adding a documented seasonal repatriation impulse

seasonality.pattern: Japanese fiscal year-end repatriation. Japanese corporates and institutions repatriate foreign earnings and rebalance portfolios for accounting purposes through late February and March, producing a documented yen-positive impulse. A secondary half-year-end pattern operates into 30 September, and the yen's outperformance of every G10 currency in September 2026 is partly consistent with it - which argues for a mechanical fade of part of that strength in early October, as the move to 158.19 on 2026-10-01 suggests.
seasonality.relevance_window: Outside the tactical 2-4 week window; squarely inside the strategic 1-6 month window, which extends to end-March 2027 and therefore captures the 2027-03-31 fiscal year-end in full.
seasonality.historical_magnitude: The February-March repatriation window has historically been worth a measurable yen-positive impulse on USD/JPY, typically concentrated in the final three weeks. The September half-year-end effect is smaller. We do not assign a point estimate because the cache carries no seasonal decomposition and we will not fabricate one.
seasonality.current_alignment: Unusually aligned. This year the seasonal flow coincides with a live structural repatriation trend driven by the hedged-yield crossover, so the two reinforce rather than merely overlap. The offsetting seasonal is December year-end dollar funding demand, which reliably widens the cross-currency basis and works against the yen in the middle of the strategic window.

assumptions: Correction issued 2026-10-05 (Fed QT). The original edition treated the Federal Reserve's 2026-09-16 implementation note as newly confirming the end of quantitative tightening and attributed the Factor 10 change to it. That was wrong: the FOMC announced on 2025-10-29 that it would conclude the reduction of its securities holdings on 2025-12-01, and the 2026-09-16 note restates reserve-management purchases already in place. Factor 10 was re-assessed on current conditions alone - stances unchanged, tactical confidence lowered from 57 to 55 and strategic from 58 to 52 - strategic overall confidence was lowered from 62 to 61, and the G10+SGD rankings were recomputed from the final net scores of all eleven dossiers.

Policy rates are taken from Data-Cache/calendar/events/ actuals for the most recent decision, not from the CBPOL_ series. This matters acutely here: the cached CBPOL_JP series ends 2026-09-22 and still reads 1.00%, two days after the BoJ's hike to 1.25% took effect. Every JPY rate differential in this dossier is computed from 1.25%, and the policy differentials embedded in the Data-Cache/derived/*.json files, which carry the stale 1.00%, are not used. The same correction applies to AUD (cached 4.35%, actual 4.60% from 2026-09-29) and NOK (cached 4.25%, actual 4.50% from 2026-09-24).

Rate conventions: EUR is quoted at the ECB deposit facility rate of 2.50% (the operational policy rate), with the 2.65% main refinancing rate noted where relevant. USD is quoted at the federal funds target range upper bound of 4.00%, with the 3.875% effective rate given alongside wherever a carry calculation depends on it. SGD has no policy rate because the MAS targets the S$NEER band; it is shown as not applicable throughout.

The cached Brent price (DCOILBRENTEU, 114.89 dollars as of 2026-09-22) is treated as corrupt and is not quoted as a live level. It sits approximately 16.7% above the market print of 98.48 dollars on 2026-10-01 and 18.48 dollars above cached WTI of 96.41, an impossible Brent-WTI relationship. Both figures are reported wherever energy prices bear on the analysis.

Japanese CPI is a documented cache gap: the OECD prices flow returns 404 for Japan at every key and FRED's redistribution ended in 2021, so JPN is absent from the vintages entirely. The August 2026 prints used here - headline 1.9%, core ex fresh food 1.7%, core-core ex fresh food and energy 1.9% - are taken from Data-Cache/calendar/events/2026-09.csv (released 2026-09-17) and confirmed against Statistics Bureau data via Trading Economics.

CPI periods in the macro comparison table are labelled individually rather than uniformly. The OECD vintages reach 2026-Q2 for the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand but only 2025-Q4 for Switzerland, Norway, Sweden and the euro area; for those four the most recent published print (August 2026) is quoted and cited instead. Singapore has no OECD vintages at all and is sourced from SingStat/MAS. Core rows are the latest published measure with the period labelled: SEK core is CPIF ex energy 0.5% (Aug 2026, Statistics Sweden via Trading Economics) and NZD core is the RBNZ sectoral factor model 2.7% (2026-Q2).

Sovereign 10-year yields from the cached IRLTLT01 series are MONTHLY and are never quoted as live. The Japanese 10-year used throughout is the live 3.05-3.07% print of 2026-09-30, not the cached 2.94% monthly observation of 2026-08-01. Where a peer 10-year is quoted from the monthly series, its vintage date is stated in the spread interpretation.

Realised volatility is read from realisedVol in Data-Cache/derived/{PAIR}.json rather than computed, and is never constructed from two USD legs. Implied volatility for USD/JPY is the CME at-the-money quoted surface observed 2026-09-25; the implied-vol surfaces shown in the cache for the JPY crosses are triangle-estimated rather than quoted and are not used in the carry-to-vol ratios, which use 60-day realised throughout.

The cross-currency basis is DERIVED, not quoted. No free source for quoted basis-swap levels exists. The approximately -21bp three-month JPY/USD basis is inferred from the cached USD/JPY futures roll premium of -296.1bp annualised against a 275bp policy differential; on the 3.875% effective rate the implied basis is approximately -34bp. It is labelled as a proxy wherever used.

Twenty-five-delta risk reversals for USD/JPY could not be sourced at the valuation date and are recorded as a documented gap. The last well-sourced print, approximately +2.8 volatility points in favour of JPY calls in late July 2026, is cited as directional context only; the implied-vol percentile of 58 is estimated from the cited 2026 range (approximately 6.0% low to 11.6% on 2026-09-09) rather than taken from a vendor percentile series.

The BoJ's 7-2 vote split is reported consistently across sources, but the characterisation of the two dissents differs: Trading Economics describes Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato as opposing faster tightening, while UPI describes them as voting to keep rates unchanged. Both readings are reported and the confidence on Factor 6 is set accordingly.

BoJ OIS pricing is taken as a directional read only. The source page returned an internally inconsistent implied-rate column (an implied 1.11% against a current 1.25% rate, with references to January and March 2026), so only the hike probabilities of approximately 25-38% for October and 39% for December are used, and they are flagged as best available.

Scheduled central-bank decision dates come exclusively from Data-Cache/calendar/central-bank-meetings.json and are never web-searched. Catalyst dates not present in that file or in the cached event store use the YYYY-MM-WN format rather than an invented exact date.

PPP deviations are estimated from the relationship between the BIS real effective exchange rates of each currency pair rather than from a published OECD PPP series, which the cache does not carry. They are directionally reliable and should not be read to a precision of better than a few percentage points.

SOFR, JKM LNG and Japanese sovereign CDS could not be sourced from free current data and are recorded as documented gaps. The US overnight funding corridor is bounded instead by the Fed's stated settings: IORB 3.90%, ON RRP 3.75% and standing repo 4.00%.

Verification outcome. Every citation URL was re-fetched at the verification stage. Three sources resolved but could not be read and were REMOVED rather than cited unverified: a Bloomberg article on the BoJ vote split (disallowed by robots.txt), a Japan Times report on the October Tankan (paywalled, HTTP 402) and a CNBC report on the joint intervention (HTTP 403). Every claim they carried is sourced elsewhere in this list - the vote split from UPI and Trading Economics, the Tankan from InvestingLive, the intervention from Al Jazeera and Wikipedia - and the citation list was renumbered sequentially after removal.

Two figures were corrected at the verification stage and the affected confidences lowered. First, the consensus USD/JPY forecast: an earlier draft cited an aggregate near 158.34 that the cited aggregator does not publish; its actual aggregate is 155.39 at one month, 153.75 at three, 151.62 at six and 145.40 by Q1 2027, which reverses the sign of the consensus divergence and is reflected throughout. Strategic overall confidence was reduced from 64 to 62 as a result. Second, the date of the coordinated intervention: sources agree on the size, the levels and the joint character but disagree on whether it was executed 2026-07-31 or in a Thursday New York session confirmed 2026-08-02/03, so the dossier describes it as late July 2026 with the discrepancy flagged, and Factor 7 confidence was reduced from 58 to 55 tactically and from 55 to 52 strategically.

The monthly snapshot used for the entire 2026-10-01 cycle is Data-Cache/2026-10/, fetched 2026-09-30T18:00:05Z, consistent with the other currencies in this cycle. The COT tranche it carries (2026-09-22) is nine days stale against the valuation date and has been refreshed from the CFTC release of 2026-09-25.
